Ohio Regulator Bans Bettor Who Threatened Blue Jays Manager Over World Series Wagers

Published October 22, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Ohio Casino Control Commission has placed an Ohio bettor, identified as Blake Morgan, on the state's involuntary sports gaming exclusion list after finding that he made harassing and threatening remarks tied to his betting activity during last year's World Series. The order bars Morgan from entering any sports gaming facility in Ohio and from taking part in sports gaming activity anywhere in the state.

What happened

According to the Commission, the case stems from a phone call Morgan made to Major League Baseball's customer service line on or around October 28, 2025, in which he directed harassing and threatening remarks at then-Blue Jays manager John Schneider, in comments the Commission linked to his sports betting activity during the 2025 World Series between the Blue Jays and the Los Angeles Dodgers. MLB responded by imposing an indefinite ban on Morgan from its stadiums, offices, and other facilities, which prompted Ohio's regulator to open its own exclusion proceeding.

Morgan requested a review of the proposed exclusion but did not appear at the hearing. A hearing examiner recommended the exclusion go forward regardless, and the Commission adopted that recommendation over Morgan's objection that an MLB investigator had implied no further action would follow. The Commission ruled that any assurances from an MLB investigator couldn't bind its own separate regulatory process. Morgan retains the right to appeal the decision through the courts.

Part of a broader enforcement push

The case lands against the backdrop of a joint push by major U.S. sports leagues for tougher state-level consequences for bettors who target athletes and team personnel. The NFL, MLB, NBA, NHL, MLS, and their players' unions sent state gaming regulators a letter in September urging mandatory lifetime bans for anyone found to have harassed or threatened players, coaches, officials, or team staff — along with a shared, cross-state reporting system so that an exclusion ordered in one state could be recognized by regulators elsewhere. The leagues argued that legal sports betting has boosted fan engagement but has also fueled a rise in abusive contact directed at people working in professional sports.

Ohio's action against Morgan doesn't yet reflect that proposed nationwide system — this exclusion applies to Ohio specifically — but it's a concrete example of a state gaming regulator acting on exactly the kind of bettor conduct the leagues' letter was written to address.

Why it matters to bettors

Most states, including Ohio, already give their gaming regulators the authority to bar a person from licensed sports wagering for conduct a sportsbook operator or the state considers harmful — this case is a reminder that an exclusion order can follow from conduct connected to betting activity even when it happens off a sportsbook's own platform, such as a phone call to a league's customer service line. Bettors in any legal state should assume that threatening or harassing conduct tied to a wager, however it's delivered, carries real regulatory risk on top of whatever a league or team itself might do in response.
